answer: Each seat ties to one numbered block in a mason's yard. Every epoch it publishes an ultrasonic transit map of a slab sawn that day from that block. The pulse signal crosses veins, vugs and hairline cracks differing even between slabs from one marble or onyx block, yet continuous along that block's cut sequence, so a map can neither be precomputed, replayed nor borrowed. A sybil must buy a genuine block per identity, run a saw, and pay a technician to shoot maps daily; these costs scale linearly and never amortise. Two seats reporting one block yield identical maps and forfeit both deposits.
